Machine Learning and the Physical Sciences

Normalizing Flows for Classical Simulation of Quantum Circuits in Phase Space

Edward Jiang Affiliation: Quantum Information Theory Group Affiliation: ICFO - Institute of Photonic Sciences Affiliation: Barcelona Institute of Science and Technology Email: ye-duo.jiang@icfo.eu    Timothy Heightman Affiliation: Quantum Information Theory Group Affiliation: ICFO - Institute of Photonic Sciences Affiliation: Barcelona Institute of Science and Technology    Marcin Płodzień Affiliation: Instytut Fizyki Teoretycznej Affiliation: Wydział Fizyki, Astronomii i Informatyki Stosowanej Affiliation: Uniwersytet Jagielloński
Abstract

We present a novel framework to learn a representation of quantum circuits based on the phase space formulation of many-body systems. Given that NN-qubit states can be represented as probability distributions on a smooth 2​N2N-dimensional manifold, we show how unitary gates can be parameterized as normalizing flows between these distributions, opening a new avenue for quantum circuit simulation using generative models. We evaluate our method on three common families of quantum circuits, and show that its accuracy exceeds that of current state-of-the-art neural network methods for large system sizes.

1 Introduction

The problem of classical simulation of quantum many-body systems is pertinent to both the existence of quantum advantage, and to inference and control of quantum hardware [1, 2]. Naive methods for classical simulation of quantum systems include exact state-vector methods and Feynman-style path integral schemes [3, 4, 5], which are simple to implement yet have an algorithmic complexity that grows exponentially in the size of the system. Other techniques exploit the structure in certain classes of quantum circuits, such as Clifford-ness [6] or low tree-rank [7, 8], which lead to efficient classical algorithms but are not applicable to other circuits. For condensed matter systems in 1D or 2D, tensor network approaches comprise the vast majority of state-of-the-art algorithms [9, 10], under the assumption that the amount of entanglement in the system is bounded by the area of any bipartition. Recently, a new class of algorithms called Pauli propagation [11, 12] has also been shown to approximately simulate quantum circuits in low magic or noisy settings.

Machine-learning techniques have also been applied to the simulation of quantum systems. Neural quantum states (NQS) and its variations [13, 14, 15, 16, 17] offer compact representations and were shown to be able to evolve nontrivial many-body states. More recently, generative models have been used to learn representations of quantum states in the probabilistic formulation of quantum dynamics [18, 19, 20]. However, the accuracy of all of these methods typically degrades with system size and evolution time.

In this paper, we present a novel method to learn the output state of a quantum circuit based on the phase space formalism of many-body qubit systems [21]. Each intermediate state is represented as a probability distribution, and unitary gates are represented as normalizing flow transformations that map from one distribution to the next. Unlike previous methods, ours is based on a continuous input space rather than a discrete domain [18, 13, 14, 15], which avoids having to use continuous relaxations or hand-crafted embeddings. In addition, our architecture is naturally composable due to the sequential nature of normalizing flows, mirroring the structure of the quantum circuit. This is in contrast with previous methods which retrain a fixed architecture variationally after each gate [16, 17, 18]. We demonstrate our method on three common families of quantum circuits, and show that the classical fidelity of our model exceeds that of two neural network baselines [14, 18] as the size and depth of the circuit grows.

2 Methods

In this section we describe our framework to learn a representation of the states in a given quantum circuit. We give a brief overview of the phase space of multi-qubit systems before describing how quantum circuits can be modeled using normalizing flows.

2.1 Phase space representation

In the phase-space formalism, NN-qubit states are represented by probability distributions over the manifold (S2)N(S^{2})^{N}, and unitary maps between states are given by a convolution with an integral kernel (or Feynman-like propagators). Although many different phase space representations exist [21], the clear choice here is the QQ function due to its positivity, and thus its interpretation as a probability distribution. For an NN-qubit state |ψ⟩{|\psi\rangle}, the QQ function of |ψ⟩{|\psi\rangle} is given by

Q|ψ⟩​(𝛀)=1(2​π)N​|⟨𝛀|ψ⟩|2\displaystyle Q_{{|\psi\rangle}}(\boldsymbol{\Omega})=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{N}}\left|\langle\boldsymbol{\Omega}|\psi\rangle\right|^{2} (1)

where 𝛀\boldsymbol{\Omega} is shorthand for (θ1,φ1,θ2,φ2,⋯,θN,φN)(\theta_{1},\varphi_{1},\theta_{2},\varphi_{2},\cdots,\theta_{N},\varphi_{N}) specifying a point on (S2)N(S^{2})^{N}, and the spin coherent states |𝛀⟩{|\boldsymbol{\Omega}\rangle} are defined as [22, 23, 24]

|𝛀⟩=⨂i=1N|Ωi⟩=⨂i=1N(cos⁡θi2​|0⟩+ei​φi​sin⁡θi2​|1⟩)\displaystyle{|\boldsymbol{\Omega}\rangle}=\bigotimes_{i=1}^{N}{|\Omega_{i}\rangle}=\bigotimes_{i=1}^{N}\left(\cos\frac{\theta_{i}}{2}{|0\rangle}+e^{i\varphi_{i}}\sin\frac{\theta_{i}}{2}{|1\rangle}\right) (2)

One can show that the QQ function is a valid probability distribution over (S2)N(S^{2})^{N} under the usual spherical measure [21] . Examples of QQ functions for some selected states are shown in App. A, see also [21].

Now suppose we have a unitary operator UU. Since UU is linear, there exists some transition kernel KU​(𝛀′,𝛀)K_{U}(\boldsymbol{\Omega^{\prime}},\boldsymbol{\Omega}) [21] such that, for any two states |ψ⟩,|ψ′⟩{|\psi\rangle},{|\psi^{\prime}\rangle} with |ψ′⟩=U​|ψ⟩{|\psi^{\prime}\rangle}=U{|\psi\rangle}, we have

Q|ψ′⟩​(𝛀′)=∫(S2)NKU​(𝛀′,𝛀)​Q|ψ⟩​(𝛀)​𝑑𝛀\displaystyle Q_{{|\psi^{\prime}\rangle}}(\boldsymbol{\Omega^{\prime}})=\int_{(S^{2})^{N}}K_{U}(\boldsymbol{\Omega^{\prime}},\boldsymbol{\Omega})\,Q_{{|\psi\rangle}}(\boldsymbol{\Omega})\,d\boldsymbol{\Omega} (3)

so that unitary maps in the Hilbert space correspond to convolution with the integral kernels KUK_{U}. Explicitly, given UU, the kernel KUK_{U} has the form

KU​(𝛀′,𝛀)\displaystyle K_{U}(\boldsymbol{\Omega^{\prime}},\boldsymbol{\Omega}) =1(2​π)N​Tr​[U†​|𝛀′⟩​⟨𝛀′|​U​Δ​(𝛀)]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{N}}\text{Tr}\left[U^{\dagger}|\boldsymbol{\Omega^{\prime}}\rangle\!\langle\boldsymbol{\Omega^{\prime}}|U\Delta(\boldsymbol{\Omega})\right] Δ⁡(𝛀)\displaystyle\Delta(\boldsymbol{\Omega}) =⨂i=1N(3​|Ωi⟩​⟨Ωi|−I)\displaystyle=\bigotimes_{i=1}^{N}\left(3|\Omega_{i}\rangle\!\langle\Omega_{i}|-I\right) (4)

Importantly, if UU only acts on a small subset SS of qubits, the integral (3) need only be performed over the coordinates Ωi\Omega_{i} with i∈Si\in S (since the non-support qubits can be integrated out analytically), so the integral can be computed efficiently in this case. Examples of transition kernels for some common unitaries UU are shown in App. B.

2.2 Quantum circuits as normalizing flows

A quantum circuit is specified by an initial state |ψ0⟩{|\psi_{0}\rangle} along with an ordered collection of gates U1,U2,⋯,UKU_{1},U_{2},\cdots,U_{K}. The state after the kk-th gate is given by

|ψk⟩=UkUk−1⋯U2U1|ψ0⟩\displaystyle{|\psi_{k}\rangle}=U_{k}U_{k-1}\cdots U_{2}U_{1}{|\psi_{0}\rangle} (5)

From the previous section, each intermediate state |ψk⟩{|\psi_{k}\rangle} can be represented as a probability distribution over (S2)N(S^{2})^{N} via Eq. (1), and mapping between states |ψk−1⟩{|\psi_{k-1}\rangle} and |ψk⟩{|\psi_{k}\rangle} is accomplished by substituting the corresponding gate UkU_{k} into Eq. (3). However, KUkK_{U_{k}} may in general contain negative values, which renders the naive efficient sampling scheme from the distribution Q|ψk⟩​(𝛀′)Q_{{|\psi_{k}\rangle}}(\boldsymbol{\Omega^{\prime}}) given Q|ψk−1⟩​(𝛀)Q_{{|\psi_{k-1}\rangle}}(\boldsymbol{\Omega}) inapplicable [20, 25]. Our solution is therefore to represent the QQ function of |ψk⟩{|\psi_{k}\rangle} as a normalizing flow using the QQ function of |ψk−1⟩{|\psi_{k-1}\rangle} as the initial distribution. More specifically, suppose that fk:(S2)N→(S2)Nf_{k}:(S^{2})^{N}\to(S^{2})^{N} is a flow transformation corresponding to UkU_{k}. Then our goal is to find fkf_{k} such that the QQ function of |ψk⟩{|\psi_{k}\rangle} is well-approximated:

Q|ψk⟩​(𝛀)≈Q~|ψk⟩​(𝛀)=Q|ψk−1⟩​(fk−1​(𝛀))​|det∂fk−1∂𝛀|\displaystyle Q_{{|\psi_{k}\rangle}}(\boldsymbol{\Omega})\approx\tilde{Q}_{{|\psi_{k}\rangle}}(\boldsymbol{\Omega})=Q_{{|\psi_{k-1}\rangle}}\left(f_{k}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\Omega})\right)\left|\det\frac{\partial f_{k}^{-1}}{\partial\boldsymbol{\Omega}}\right| (6)

with the right-hand-side being the usual change-of-variables formula for the probability density [26]. This process is composable: to approximate the QQ function for a state |ψk⟩{|\psi_{k}\rangle}, we can pushforward the QQ function for the initial state |ψ0⟩{|\psi_{0}\rangle} through each of the flows f1,f2,⋯,fkf_{1},f_{2},\cdots,f_{k} in order.

We emphasize that the QQ function is a distribution over an 2​N2N-dimensional manifold, and thus the normalizing flows can be implemented efficiently. The problem of the exponential growth of the Hilbert space is now a problem of model expressivity [14, 13].

The initial state |ψ0⟩{|\psi_{0}\rangle} is usually some fiducial state, which can be taken to be |00⋯0⟩{|00\cdots 0\rangle}. This has the simple product QQ function given by (see also App. A):

Q|ψ0⟩​(𝛀)=∏i=1NQ|0⟩​(Ωi)=1(4​π)N​∏i=1N(1+cos⁡θi)\displaystyle Q_{{|\psi_{0}\rangle}}(\boldsymbol{\Omega})=\prod_{i=1}^{N}Q_{{|0\rangle}}(\Omega_{i})=\frac{1}{(4\pi)^{N}}\prod_{i=1}^{N}(1+\cos\theta_{i}) (7)

where, importantly, sampling and computing likelihoods are both efficient and exact. We parameterize each flow fkf_{k} with trainable parameters αk\alpha_{k}, and train to minimize the KL divergence between the QQ functions obtained via the transition kernel (3) and the ones given by the trainable flows:

ℒ(𝜶)=∑k=1K𝒟(∫KUk(𝛀′,𝛀)Q~|ψk−1⟩(𝛀)d𝛀∥Q~|ψk⟩(𝛀;αk))\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\alpha})=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathcal{D}\left(\int K_{U_{k}}(\boldsymbol{\Omega^{\prime}},\boldsymbol{\Omega})\,\tilde{Q}_{{|\psi_{k-1}\rangle}}(\boldsymbol{\Omega})\,d\boldsymbol{\Omega}\,\,\bigg\|\,\,\tilde{Q}_{{|\psi_{k}\rangle}}\left(\boldsymbol{\Omega};\alpha_{k}\right)\right) (8)

where Q~|ψk⟩\tilde{Q}_{{|\psi_{k}\rangle}} is the model’s approximation of Q|ψk⟩Q_{|\psi_{k}\rangle}, and Q~|ψ0⟩=Q|ψ0⟩\tilde{Q}_{{|\psi_{0}\rangle}}=Q_{|\psi_{0}\rangle}. Assuming each gate UkU_{k} acts on a small number of qubits, the KL divergences can be estimated efficiently using Monte Carlo sampling; the kk-th term requires samples from the k−1k-1-th QQ function, which can be obtained efficiently due to the composability of normalizing flows. Thus training uses only the learned QQ functions, and the exact QQ functions are used only to evaluate the trained model.

In practice, we pre-train each of the flows sequentially from k=1k=1 to k=Kk=K for better stability in the early stages of training, and then fine-tune all flows jointly on Eq. 8. Our framework is illustrated in Fig. 1.

2.3 Related work

Normalizing flows have also been applied to quantum systems directly. Closest to our work is Q-Flow [27], which likewise represents the Husimi QQ function with a normalizing flow, but for open continuous-variable systems: the phase space is ℝ2​N\mathbb{R}^{2N}, and the flow is evolved in continuous time under the PDE that the Lindblad dynamics induces for QQ. Flows have also been used as neural quantum states for continuous-variable many-body systems [28], and flow matching on spin Wigner functions has been used to learn distributions over multi-qubit states [29]. Our setting differs in three ways. First, we treat qubits, whose phase space is the compact manifold (S2)N(S^{2})^{N}. Second, the dynamics is a sequence of discrete gates, whose phase-space action is a convolution rather than a differential operator. Third, instead of re-fitting or evolving a single flow, we assign one flow per gate and compose them.

3 Experiments

To evaluate our framework, we train normalizing flow models for three families of quantum circuits: 1D cluster state preparation, GHZ state preparation, and ground state preparation of a 1D transverse-field Ising model (TFIM) at the critical point. These are the same families of circuits that were used for evaluation in [18].

For our normalizing flow architecture, we use a continuous normalizing flow [30, 31] over the manifold (S2)N(S^{2})^{N} for each unitary operator, using a simple multi-layer perceptron (MLP) to parameterize the vector field. We train on the loss function in equation (8) with the Adam optimizer [32] with learning rate 0.001 until convergence.

Nothing in our method uses the Clifford structure of the GHZ and cluster circuits. They were chosen because exact QQ functions are available at large NN, and to allow direct comparison with [18]. In contrast, the VQE circuit contains arbitrary-angle rotations and is not Clifford.

We evaluate the trained model by computing the classical fidelity between the QQ function of the true state Q|ψK⟩Q_{|\psi_{K}\rangle} and the final predicted distribution Q~\tilde{Q}:

F⁡(Q|ψK⟩,Q~)=∫(S2)NQ|ψK⟩​(𝛀)​Q~​(𝛀)​𝑑𝛀\displaystyle F\left(Q_{|\psi_{K}\rangle},\tilde{Q}\right)=\int_{(S^{2})^{N}}\sqrt{Q_{|\psi_{K}\rangle}(\boldsymbol{\Omega})\tilde{Q}(\boldsymbol{\Omega})}\,d\boldsymbol{\Omega} (9)

since it is efficient to estimate for large system sizes (whereas computing the quantum fidelity is intractable). We compare against the results in [18], which uses a transformer architecture to learn the IC-POVM probability vector of a state instead of the QQ function, and evaluates it using the discrete version of the classical fidelity (9). We pull the metrics directly from [18]. For the 1D cluster state and GHZ state, we also benchmark against neural quantum states (NQS) [14], which uses the TDVP algorithm to find optimal parameters that solve the dynamics. In this case, we run the training routine from scratch, using an MLP to parameterize the real and imaginary parts of the wavefunction and the stochastic reconfiguration algorithm for TDVP time-stepping.

The results are shown in Figures 2 and 3. At the largest sizes, our model reaches F≈0.96F\approx 0.96 at N=64N=64 for the cluster state, compared with 0.910.91 (IC-POVM) and 0.840.84 (NQS) at N=60N=60, and F≈0.965F\approx 0.965 for the GHZ state, compared with 0.950.95 (IC-POVM) and 0.960.96 (NQS). For the VQE circuit, we see that the fidelity decreases roughly linearly by ∼3×10−4\sim 3\times 10^{-4} per gate, reaching 0.9850.985 compared with 0.9650.965 for the transformer.

4 Discussion and limitations

Computational cost.

Each gate has its own flow, so the number of parameters grows linearly with the number of gates KK. Training gate kk requires evaluating Q~k−1\tilde{Q}_{k-1} at new points, which means inverting the k−1k-1 preceding flows, so the total training cost grows as 𝒪⁡(K2)\mathcal{O}(K^{2}). In contrast, the baseline neural methods retrain a fixed-size model after each gate, so their total training cost grows as 𝒪⁡(K)\mathcal{O}(K). As a result, Figures 2 and 3 compare accuracy at a given system size and are not compute-matched.

Negativity.

The model is necessary in the first place because the transition kernels KUkK_{U_{k}} generally contain negative values. Despite this, convolution with the kernel can be computed efficiently assuming that UkU_{k} only has support on a small number of qubits (say 2), since the unsupported coordinates can be integrated out analytically. On the other hand, simulating the whole circuit as a single unitary gate would require integrating over all 2​N2N coordinates. Thus the sign problem manifests as approximation error of the learned model, which compounds exponentially with the circuit depth (see Figure 3).

State dependence.

For a single-qubit gate UU acting on qubit ii, the QQ function transforms exactly via the rotation RUR_{U} that UU induces on the ii-th Bloch sphere. Hence fk=RUkf_{k}=R_{U_{k}} is an exact flow that is independent of the input, including for non-Clifford gates such as TT. For entangling gates however, no such flow exists in general. Each learned fkf_{k} is therefore an approximate transport map from Q~k−1\tilde{Q}_{k-1} to its convolution with KUkK_{U_{k}}. For a different input state Q^k−1\hat{Q}_{k-1}, the transport map does not carry over and would need to be retrained.

5 Conclusion and outlook

In this contribution, we introduced a novel framework to learn the output state of a quantum circuit based on normalizing flows in the phase space representation, and showed numerically that the method is able to scale well to large system sizes.

Natural next benchmarks are Trotterized dynamics e−i​H​te^{-iHt} of local Hamiltonians, in regimes that challenge tensor networks and Pauli propagation, as well as noisy and open-system evolution [33]. Since local observables can be estimated from flow samples, the composed flow could also serve as a variational ansatz: one would optimize the gate parameters of a circuit using energies estimated through the flows.

Appendix A QQ Functions of Selected States

Recall that the QQ function is defined as

Q|ψ⟩​(𝛀)=1(2​π)N​|⟨𝛀|ψ⟩|2\displaystyle Q_{{|\psi\rangle}}(\boldsymbol{\Omega})=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{N}}\left|\langle\boldsymbol{\Omega}|\psi\rangle\right|^{2} (10)

where 𝛀=(θ1,φ1,θ2,φ2,⋯,θN,φN)\boldsymbol{\Omega}=(\theta_{1},\varphi_{1},\theta_{2},\varphi_{2},\cdots,\theta_{N},\varphi_{N}), and the coherent state |𝛀⟩{|\boldsymbol{\Omega}\rangle} is given by

|𝛀⟩=(cosθ12|0⟩+ei​φ1sinθ12|1⟩)⊗⋯⊗(cosθN2|0⟩+ei​φNsinθN2|1⟩)\displaystyle{|\boldsymbol{\Omega}\rangle}=\left(\cos\frac{\theta_{1}}{2}{|0\rangle}+e^{i\varphi_{1}}\sin\frac{\theta_{1}}{2}{|1\rangle}\right)\otimes\cdots\otimes\left(\cos\frac{\theta_{N}}{2}{|0\rangle}+e^{i\varphi_{N}}\sin\frac{\theta_{N}}{2}{|1\rangle}\right) (11)

In Table 1 we show the QQ functions for the eigenstates of the single-qubit Pauli operators, the four 2-qubit Bell states, and the 3-qubit GHZ and W states.

Appendix B Transition Kernels of Selected Unitaries

Recall that the transition kernel KU​(𝛀′,𝛀)K_{U}(\boldsymbol{\Omega^{\prime}},\boldsymbol{\Omega}) of a unitary UU is defined as

Q|ψ′⟩​(𝛀′)=∫(S2)NKU​(𝛀′,𝛀)​Q|ψ⟩​(𝛀)​𝑑𝛀\displaystyle Q_{{|\psi^{\prime}\rangle}}(\boldsymbol{\Omega^{\prime}})=\int_{(S^{2})^{N}}K_{U}(\boldsymbol{\Omega^{\prime}},\boldsymbol{\Omega})\,Q_{{|\psi\rangle}}(\boldsymbol{\Omega})\,d\boldsymbol{\Omega} (12)

for all states |ψ⟩,|ψ′⟩{|\psi\rangle},{|\psi^{\prime}\rangle} such that |ψ′⟩=U​|ψ⟩{|\psi^{\prime}\rangle}=U{|\psi\rangle}. In Table 2 we show the kernels for the Pauli X,Y,ZX,Y,Z and HH gates, as well as an arbitrary ZZ rotation and the two-qubit controlled ZZ gate. Altogether these operators form a universal set of gates.
